lesson.menu_title: What Do You Think? — An Opinion That Holds Up
lesson.menu_desc: Saying what you think and backing it up with because, so, but and that's why -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- What Do You Think?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Giovanna Waltrick | Lesson 12 -- What Do You Think?
lesson.grammar_point: connectors because, so, but and that's why to support an opinion

listenings.text: I buy clothes for a store in the city center, and every season somebody asks me the same question: should we follow the trends or not? My answer is always the same. A trend-driven piece sells fast, but it also stops selling fast. Six weeks later it is on sale, and nobody wants it. So I keep two lists. The first list is small, and it changes every month. The second list is long, and it is full of versatile pieces, the ones that work with a jacket, with jeans and with a dress. That second list pays the rent. For example, we have sold the same black pants for nine years. Nobody posts a photo of them. That's why I never argue against trends completely. I just never let them choose the whole store for me.

The question for today's episode is simple: what matters more, style or sustainability? My answer is not the popular one. In my opinion, they are not two sides. When a piece is versatile, you wear it more, so you buy less. That is sustainability, and nobody needs to give a speech about it. The reason I care is practical, not moral. I have a small budget, so every choice has to work hard. For example, last year I bought one good jacket instead of four cheap ones. I still wear it every week, but I do not think of it as a green decision. I think of it as good value. That's why I prefer to talk about style first. People listen to style, and sustainability comes with it.
